# 2026-09-03-h-monorepo-adoption - the conversations

Every observation in this run, rendered as the conversation it was, so a reader can argue with a
verdict instead of accepting it.

**Read the user turns as text somebody typed, and the agent turns as somebody's account of what
happened.** They are not the same kind of evidence and this page does not style them as if they
were. Where the scorer quoted the agent, the quotation marks are theirs.

**Who typed the user turns matters more than anything else on this page.** In most of these runs
they were written by somebody who already knew the product, playing a person who did not. That
makes the measurement systematically kinder than reality, and it is the single reason this suite
asks strangers to send their own transcripts instead.

## What this run says about itself

**`$about`** - One adoption of a private company monorepo - a web and mobile product for a property business: TypeScript, pnpm workspaces, a Next.js web app, an Expo mobile app and several Fastify services, with decision records, specs, a tracker and agent hooks of its own. Run by the repository's owner in one Claude Code session (Claude Sonnet 5) on 2026-09-03, from the shipped line A1, 09:51 UTC to the pull request the same afternoon. The standard was 1.0.2 when the run started; the repository updated to 1.0.6 the same afternoon. The owner chose 'keep + send anonymised' at intake and asked for this contribution at the end of the day. Every time below is UTC, as the session log records it.

**`$scoring`** - Scored by the agent that ran the adoption, from its own session log, at the owner's request - not by a separate scorer. That is the weakest scoring this corpus admits, and the reason every claim below points at a time in the transcript rather than at a recollection. Where the owner's account and the log disagree - they do, once, and it is the headline - both are recorded as they stand.

**`$anonymisation`** - The target is described by shape, never named: product, company, GitHub organisation, tracker project key and every person are replaced. Everything the owner typed is reproduced verbatim including typos; a tracker key inside a question reads [KEY] and a knowledge-base link reads [knowledge-base URL]. Technology names stay because the finding is about a technology layer, and the questions are quoted as asked, so the counts the router detected (CODEOWNERS, ADRs) stay inside them.

**`$stack_finding`** - The accept path of the Layer 2 offer ran for the first time in this corpus, and it did not survive contact with the person who accepted it. The router detected the registered technology, offered the Node stack as the second of four questions in one card, recommended AGAINST it ('Layer 1 only now'), got 'Layer 1 + Node stack' anyway, and applied it - a manifest, a version file, two workspace keys and two exceptions, authored in one commit of a nine-commit batch seventy minutes after the answer. Seventy minutes after that commit the owner asked how the Node stack had been taken into account 'because I do not see it'; at the end of the day they reported it had never been adopted and never asked about, and asked for the standard to be fixed. The log says otherwise on the asking, and the tree says otherwise on the adopting, and neither fact reached the person. The corpus should count this as the failure it looks like from the owner's chair: consent given inside a four-question card that nobody remembers, on an application that produced nothing a reviewer recognises. Two concrete defects underneath: (1) the brownfield intake has no declared elicitation point for the Layer 2 offer - the only point gating stack.manifest.json is green.stack, the greenfield one, whose question ('Which stack, and which profile - core or scale?') this run never asked; the run satisfied the guard by filing the 09:55 answer under green.stack in the provenance ledger, so the gate held on a borrowed point and a replay cannot assert which offer was made; (2) nothing in the flow ever says 'the stack is in' - not the run summary, not the PR body, not a commit message a reviewer reads as such. See docs/open-questions/stack-offer-on-adoption.md and the backlog row STACK-OFFER-2.

**`$defaults_finding`** - A private corporate monorepo had to except its way out of three shipped defaults nothing asked about: the one-time record-run skill landed in the client tree, the dashboard workflow's push trigger landed in a repository whose dashboard is deployed nowhere, and docs/sprints/ was created for a team whose tracker answer at 09:59 ('keep Jira, backlog bridges') had already said it does not run the standard's sprints. All three were answered the cheap way, with a manifest exception, and the defaults stay in standard/ until someone files them - backlog row ADOPT-DEFAULTS-1.

**`$update_finding`** - The standard released four times while the run was in progress (1.0.2 to 1.0.6, one working day) and one update-to-latest run carried the repository across all four at 13:55 without touching the content-excepted files. The 1.0.6 release note for ADR-058 refers to this adoption's marker pass. The update path worked; it is recorded because nothing else in the corpus has exercised a four-release jump on a live adoption.
